pitfalls: Assuming YAML's `steps:` lists are one flat sequence — EIPs like choice, split, and filter each open their own nested `steps:` scope, and a step placed at the wrong indentation level silently attaches to the wrong branch (YAML's version of forgetting Java's end()).

Treating 'XML DSL' as a single format — mixing Camel's framework-agnostic XML IO `<routes>` document with a classic Spring `<camelContext>` wrapper fails schema validation, since each uses its own XSD and namespace and neither root element accepts the other's wrapper.

Picking YAML purely because it feels modern rather than because the route benefits from being data — a route with heavy conditional logic hand-generated in YAML with templating hacks is worse than the same logic expressed directly in Java's real loops and conditionals (Chapter 06).

Assuming a legacy Spring-XML-based Camel application should be rewritten into YAML or Java before it can be touched — the pragmatic path for extending an app that already runs on classic Spring XML is usually to keep extending it in that same DSL, not to force a rewrite just to modernize the syntax.

claims.text: An Exchange (org.apache.camel.Exchange) carries four things through one route execution, not just a message: the current Message (body + headers), a separate exchange-scoped property map, an ExchangePattern (does this step expect a reply?), and — once something has gone wrong — an exception. All four live on the same Exchange instance for the exchange's whole lifetime; nothing about them is reconstructed mid-route.

Historic Camel exposed a dual getIn()/getOut() message model (an 'In' message for what arrived, an 'Out' message for a step's reply), and both methods still exist for backward compatibility, but both are lazy-creating: calling getOut() when no out message exists silently creates an empty one rather than returning null, which is why checking hasOut() (not getOut() != null) was the historic idiom for 'did this step actually produce a reply'. Modern Camel (3.x/4.x) replaced this with a single current Message reached via getMessage() — the model this book uses throughout — and getOut() is deprecated in its favor.

A Message's body is untyped (a plain Object) until something asks it to be a type: calling message.getBody(SomeType.class) hands the request to Camel's type-converter registry (DefaultTypeConverter), which searches its loaded converters — sourced from whatever's on the classpath — for one that can turn the body's actual runtime type into the requested type, and performs the conversion on demand. Calling the no-arg getBody() never converts; it just returns whatever object is currently stored.

If no registered converter can bridge the body's actual type to the requested type, getBody(Class) throws NoTypeConversionAvailableException at the point of the call, not earlier — a route can carry a body of the 'wrong' type through several steps with no error until a step finally demands a type nothing can produce it from.

Message headers are stored in a case-insensitive map by default (Camel's CaseInsensitiveMap, selected via the pluggable HeadersMapFactory on CamelContext): header("contenttype"), header("ContentType"), and header("CONTENTTYPE") all resolve to the same entry. This mirrors how HTTP and mail headers are conventionally treated, and Camel's own header() language performs its lookup the same case-insensitive way.

Exchange properties are a second key/value store, separate from headers, managed through exchange.setProperty()/getProperty()/getProperties()/removeProperty()/hasProperties() rather than through the Message at all. Scope is the whole distinction: a header rides with the current Message and can be dropped or replaced the moment an EIP builds a new Message (Splitter, Multicast, Enrich all do this per branch); an exchange property is attached to the Exchange itself and survives across those same steps, which is why routing-internal bookkeeping (an original-body backup, a correlation id used only inside the route) belongs on a property, not a header.

Camel itself writes to reserved exchange properties as a route runs — e.g. Exchange.EXCEPTION_CAUGHT ("CamelExceptionCaught") holds the exception an onException block is currently handling — so exchange properties aren't only a developer's scratch space; some carry framework-set routing state a route can read (and should not casually overwrite).

ExchangePattern (an enum with InOnly and InOut as the two patterns used in practice) governs whether a step expects a reply. InOnly is a one-way, fire-and-forget send — publish and move on, no response expected. InOut is request-reply — the caller blocks for a response (an HTTP call, a bean method invocation with a return value). Each endpoint has a sensible default set by its component (HTTP and bean calls default to InOut; JMS, file, and most messaging-style endpoints default to InOnly), and code can override it explicitly by calling exchange.setPattern(ExchangePattern.InOut) or via .to(ExchangePattern.InOut, "...") in the DSL.

When a Processor (built-in EIP or custom code) throws, Camel does not propagate the exception up the JVM call stack as a normal exception in the route's flow — it catches it and calls exchange.setException(cause), storing it on the Exchange itself. exchange.isFailed() then reports true (equivalent to checking exchange.getException() != null), and Camel's error handler machinery — Dead Letter Channel by default, covered in Part VI — is what actually inspects that exception and decides what happens next (retry, redirect to a dead letter destination, or let it propagate).

Once an onException block (or a doTry/doCatch block) has claimed an exception, exchange.getException() reads as null again inside that block and downstream of it — the exception has been 'handled', not merely observed. The same Throwable is still reachable, just relocated: it's available as the exchange property Exchange.EXCEPTION_CAUGHT ("CamelExceptionCaught") for the rest of the route, e.g. via ${exception.message} in Simple, or exchange.getProperty(Exchange.EXCEPTION_CAUGHT, Throwable.class) in code.

snippets.note: getBody(Class)/getHeader(name, Class) both go through the type-converter registry; setProperty is on the Exchange, not the Message.
Overriding the exchange pattern on a single .to() call — bean invocations default to InOut anyway, but the explicit form is how any step is forced into request-reply.

The exception moves from getException() to the CamelExceptionCaught property the moment onException claims it. Part VI covers onException's full syntax; this page only shows where the exception itself ends up.

pitfalls: Calling exchange.getOut() (or the older getIn()) 'just to check' whether a reply exists — both lazily create an empty message the instant they're called, so the check itself creates the very thing being tested for. getMessage() plus exchange.getPattern() is the reliable modern equivalent.

Assuming a body survives untouched until proven otherwise — getBody(Class) only fails at the moment a step demands an unconvertible type, so a NoTypeConversionAvailableException can surface several steps downstream of the code that actually put the 'wrong' object in the body, far from where the real bug is.

Relying on header name casing to distinguish two logically different values (e.g. treating OrderId and orderId as separate headers) — Camel's default CaseInsensitiveMap folds them into the same entry, so the second write silently overwrites the first.

Reading exchange.getException() after an onException or doCatch block has already run — it's null by design at that point (the exception was 'handled'), and the original Throwable has to be read from the Exchange.EXCEPTION_CAUGHT property instead.

Sending to an InOnly-only endpoint (a plain JMS/file producer) and then reading exchange.getMessage() expecting a response — there isn't one; InOnly is fire-and-forget, and the 'current message' after the call is unchanged, not a reply.

claims.text: Camel offers three distinct tools for changing what's in a message, each suited to a different weight of transformation: the Simple language for short inline expressions evaluated directly in the DSL (setBody, setHeader, filter, choice/when, transform); the bean component for delegating a transformation to an existing plain Java method; and a custom Processor for logic too involved for either — arbitrary Java with full access to the Exchange.

setBody() and transform() are both Message Translator EIP steps that replace the current message's body with the result of an expression — in modern Camel's single-current-message model (Chapter 08) there is no meaningful difference left between 'the In body' and 'the Out body' for either step to disagree about; the historic distinction (transform() was documented as always setting the Out message, back when Exchange carried separate In/Out messages) predates the getMessage() model this book uses throughout. In practice setBody() is the everyday choice; transform() exists as the same operation named after the pattern it implements, and both accept any Expression (Simple, a lambda, another language).

setHeader(name, expression) is setBody's sibling for message metadata: it evaluates an expression and stores the result under a header key on the current message, rather than replacing the body — the two are frequently used together (compute a value once with .process(), stash it as a header, and route or log against it downstream).

convertBodyTo(Class) is a dedicated EIP for the narrow case of 'just change the body's Java type, don't compute a new value' — it hands the current body to the type-converter registry and replaces it with the converted result, which is shorter and more declarative in a route than a one-line .process() calling exchange.getMessage().getBody(SomeType.class) by hand.

The Simple language mixes plain literal text with ${...} expression markers freely in one string — anything outside ${} is copied through unchanged, and each ${} block is evaluated and substituted, which is what a call like log("Copying ${header.CamelFileName}") (Chapter 05) has been doing since the first route in this book.

Simple's built-in functions read every part of the Exchange this book has covered by name: ${body} (the current message body), ${header.name} (a header, matched case-insensitively per Chapter 08), ${exchangeProperty.name} (an exchange property — dot, colon, or bracket notation all work: exchangeProperty.color, exchangeProperty:color, exchangeProperty[color]), and ${body.someGetter} for reaching into a POJO body via its accessor (${body.address.city} calls getAddress().getCity()).

As a predicate language (used inside filter(), choice()/when(), and anywhere else a route needs a true/false decision), Simple supports comparison and string operators — ==, >, <, >=, <=, !=, contains, in, is, range, regex among others. The left-hand value must be a ${...} expression; the right-hand value may be a string literal in single quotes, a constant, null, or another ${...} expression, and spaces are required around the operator. Camel automatically type-converts the right-hand value to the left-hand value's type before comparing, which is why ${header.OrderTotal} > 100 works even though a header value arriving over HTTP or JMS is very often a String underneath.

The same Content-Based Router and Filter EIPs from Chapter 03 accept a predicate two ways: the fluent Java DSL builder (header("CamelOrderCountry").isEqualTo("US")), which is type-checked and refactorable, or an equivalent Simple string ("${header.CamelOrderCountry} == 'US'") passed to simple(...), which is shorter and is the only option available in the YAML/XML DSLs (Chapter 07), where there's no Java builder to call.

A Message's body is untyped (Chapter 08): getBody(Class) hands the request to Camel's type-converter registry, which is populated at startup by scanning the classpath for META-INF/services/org/apache/camel/TypeConverterLoader files contributed by every Camel component JAR present — the reason type conversions between, say, a String and an InputStream just work with no explicit configuration is that camel-core and its components ship these converter loaders already.

A custom type converter is an ordinary class annotated @Converter, with each conversion method (a static method taking the from-type, optionally a second Exchange parameter, and returning the to-type) also annotated @Converter — the Camel build tooling (or, historically, reflection at runtime) turns each annotated pair into an entry in the registry. @Converter(generateLoader = true) on the class, combined with the Camel component packaging plugin, generates the TypeConverterLoader file at build time instead of relying on reflective scanning, which is the faster, recommended path for new code. A separate @FallbackConverter method can be registered to run only after every regular converter has already failed to produce the requested type.

The bean component (bean:beanName or the .bean(...) DSL shortcut) invokes a plain Java object already registered in Camel's registry (a Spring/Quarkus/CDI bean, or one registered manually), converting the current message body to whatever type the chosen method's parameter declares and replacing the message body with the method's return value — no Camel-specific interface or import required on the POJO itself.

Camel resolves which method to invoke on a bean, in order of precedence: (1) an explicit method name given in the DSL (.bean("pricingService", "quote") or bean:pricingService?method=quote), (2) a header named CamelBeanMethodName set on the message, (3) a method the bean itself marks with Camel's @Handler annotation, and only after all of those, (4) Camel's own best-effort resolution among the bean's public methods by matching the message body's type against each candidate's parameter type. Parameter types can be qualified explicitly (bean:foo?method=bar(String,int)) to disambiguate an overloaded method, and literal parameter values can be supplied directly in the method option for methods that don't need the message body at all.

Because a bean-invoked method is ordinary Java with no Exchange or Camel type in its signature, it is trivially unit-testable on its own, outside any route — which is the main practical argument for pulling non-trivial transformation logic into a bean method rather than an inline .process() lambda: the same code exercised by the route can also be exercised directly by a plain unit test.

snippets.note: setHeader/filter/setBody all driven by Simple expressions — the same predicate machinery Chapter 03's choice()/filter() used, written inline instead of with the fluent header(...) builder.
The bean has no Camel imports at all. Camel converts the current body to Order (PricingService.quote's parameter type), invokes quote(), and replaces the body with the returned Quote.

A hand-written converter: annotate the class and the static method, declare the from-type as the first parameter and the to-type as the return type. Once on the classpath, getBody(Order.class) can produce an Order from a String body with no route-level code change.
convertBodyTo is the declarative shortcut for a type-only change — equivalent to, but shorter than, a .process() lambda that calls getBody(String.class) and writes it back.

pitfalls: Reaching for a raw .process() lambda for every transformation out of habit — a one-line body/header change is almost always clearer as setBody()/setHeader() with a Simple expression, and a POJO-shaped transformation is almost always more testable as a bean method; save .process() for logic that genuinely needs a full Exchange and imperative Java.

Writing a Simple predicate without spaces around the operator (${header.Total}>100) — the language requires spaces around the operator to parse correctly; the compact form is easy to type from habit with other languages and fails to parse the way it looks like it should.

Forgetting that the right-hand side of a Simple comparison needs quotes for a string literal ('US', not US) — an unquoted bare word is treated as another expression to evaluate, not a literal, and the predicate silently doesn't do what was intended rather than failing to compile (Simple expressions are only checked at route-build/runtime, not by the Java compiler).

Relying on Camel's best-effort bean method resolution (matching the body's type against overloaded methods) instead of naming the method explicitly — it works until a second overload is added later that also happens to accept a compatible type, at which point which method actually runs becomes ambiguous and can silently change; an explicit method name or an @Handler annotation removes the ambiguity for good.

Assuming a bean method's return value is optional — the bean component always replaces the current message body with whatever the invoked method returns, including a void method's null, which quietly wipes out a body a later step still expected to read.

Choosing convertBodyTo(Class) when the transformation actually needs to compute or reshape a value, not just change its Java representation — convertBodyTo only calls the type-converter registry; anything that isn't a registered conversion (renaming a field, combining two values) needs setBody()/transform() or a bean/processor instead.

claims.text: Marshal and Unmarshal are dedicated EIPs, distinct from the type-converter registry (Chapters 08–09): marshal(dataFormat) turns the current message body — typically a Java object — into a binary or textual wire format ready to be sent over the network; unmarshal(dataFormat) does the reverse, turning received wire-format data back into a Java object. Both delegate to a pluggable DataFormat implementation rather than to getBody(Class)/convertBodyTo.

A Data Format is a named, pluggable component behind marshal()/unmarshal() — Camel ships dozens of them (JSON via several libraries, XML via JAXB, CSV via Apache Commons CSV, plus YAML, Avro, Protobuf and more), each configured the same two ways: a short fluent DSL call (marshal().json(), unmarshal().csv()) or a named, reusable DataFormat instance/registry entry that can be defined once and referenced by id from multiple routes — the same 'define once, reuse everywhere' shape Chapter 09's converters used.

JSON in Camel is library-pluggable rather than built into camel-core: Jackson, Gson, Johnzon and (historically) XStream are all supported, selected explicitly with a JsonLibrary argument — marshal().json(JsonLibrary.Jackson) — or implicitly by which json dataformat dependency is on the classpath. Jackson is the library used throughout this book's examples, via the camel-jackson dependency and the JacksonDataFormat/.json(JsonLibrary.Jackson, SomeClass.class) DSL form.

unmarshalType tells Jackson which Java class to deserialize JSON into; when it is left unset, Camel does not fail — it deserializes into a generic java.util.Map (or a List of Maps for a JSON array) instead of a typed POJO, which is convenient for quick inspection but means a route that assumes a specific POJO type downstream will get a ClassCastException instead of the object it expects.

Data formats implement a shared, optional contentTypeHeader behavior (the DataFormatContentTypeHeader marker) that, when enabled, sets the message's Content-Type header to the format's MIME type immediately after marshalling — application/json for the JSON formats, application/xml for JAXB — so a route that marshals straight onto an HTTP or messaging endpoint doesn't need a separate setHeader step just to label what it's sending.

JAXB is Camel's standard XML data format: JaxbDataFormat marshals JAXB-annotated Java classes (or classes generated by XJC from an XSD) to XML and back, configured with a contextPath naming the package to scan for JAXB classes rather than a single class — one JaxbDataFormat instance can marshal/unmarshal every JAXB class in that package. An optional schema (one or more XSD locations) turns on schema validation during marshalling and unmarshalling, failing the exchange on invalid XML instead of silently accepting it.

The CSV data format wraps Apache Commons CSV. marshal() accepts a Map (or anything Camel can convert to one) per row and writes a CSV line; unmarshal() by default produces a List of Lists — one inner List<String> of field values per CSV row, with no notion of column names. Setting useMaps(true) changes unmarshal's shape to a List<Map<String,String>> instead, treating the first row as a header line and using its values as each map's keys — the difference between reading a row positionally (get(0), get(1)) and reading it by column name (get("OrderId")).

The YAML DSL mirrors the Java DSL's shape for data formats one-for-one: a marshal or unmarshal step names the format and nests its options under it (marshal: / json: / library: Jackson / unmarshalType: com.example.Order), the same 'format name, then format-specific options' structure Chapter 07 already showed for other EIPs — there is no Java-only capability here that YAML lacks.

snippets.note: unmarshalType (Order.class) is what makes the result a typed Order instead of a generic Map.
marshal().json() with no unmarshalType needed — marshalling only ever needs to know the source object, never a target type.
contextPath names the package to scan for JAXB-annotated classes, not a single class — one instance handles every JAXB class in that package.
Default unmarshal() shape is a List<List<String>> — split(body()) hands each inner List (one CSV row) to processRow in turn.
useMaps(true) switches the row shape to Map<String,String>, so a row reads by header name (OrderId, Total) instead of numeric position.

pitfalls: Reaching for convertBodyTo(String.class) or a hand-rolled ObjectMapper call to get JSON out of a POJO instead of marshal().json() — convertBodyTo only calls the type-converter registry from Chapter 09, which has no built-in POJO-to-JSON converter; marshal/unmarshal are the purpose-built EIPs for whole-message format conversion and are the idiomatic tool for this job.

Leaving unmarshalType unset on a JSON unmarshal step and being surprised later by a ClassCastException — Camel quietly hands back a generic Map instead of failing at the unmarshal step itself, so the type mismatch surfaces downstream, away from its actual cause.

Assuming CSV unmarshal() gives column-name access by default — without useMaps(true) the result is a List<List<String>> read by numeric position; a route written against ${body[OrderId]}-style access will fail unless useMaps is turned on.

Marshalling a JAXB class with no @XmlRootElement (and no wrapping JAXBElement) — JAXB needs to know the root element name and namespace to write valid XML, and this only fails at route-run time, not at compile time, so the mistake surfaces as a runtime exception on the first message, not a build error.

Treating unmarshal-then-marshal as a byte-for-byte round trip — element/attribute ordering, whitespace, and namespace declarations can all shift, so don't rely on this pairing to reproduce an original payload exactly (e.g. for hash comparison or audit logging).

claims.text: The Validate EIP (validate(predicate)) checks a message against a Predicate or Expression and throws a PredicateValidationException the moment it evaluates false. It needs no schema and no annotated class — just a boolean check inline in the route, the same predicate machinery Chapter 03's choice()/filter() and Chapter 09's Simple expressions already use, which makes it the lightest of the validation tools this chapter covers.

The Validator component (validator:resourceUri) performs XML Schema (XSD) validation via JAXP: resourceUri points to an XSD on the classpath, filesystem, or a remote URL, the parsed Schema is cached for reuse across messages, and a message that fails validation throws a validation exception instead of continuing through the route. The JMX operation clearCachedSchema forces the cached schema to be re-read on the next message, useful if the XSD file itself changes at runtime.

camel-jaxb's JaxbDataFormat (Chapter 10) can validate as part of marshalling/unmarshalling instead of as a separate step: giving it one or more XSD locations via its schema option turns on schema validation in both directions, so malformed XML fails the exchange immediately at the unmarshal step rather than being silently accepted or partially salvaged.

The JSON Schema Validator component (json-validator:resourceUri) validates a JSON message body against a JSON Schema document, supporting draft v4, v6, v7, 2019-09, and 2020-12 (partial), using the NetworkNT json-schema-validator library. It has been available since Camel 2.20 and, unlike the XML Validator component, is producer-only — it's always used as a .to("json-validator:...") step partway through a route, never as the route's from(...).

The Bean Validator component (bean-validator://label) validates a Java object already sitting in the message body against Jakarta Bean Validation (JSR 380) annotations declared on its class — @NotNull, @Size, and the rest — using Hibernate Validator as the default provider. By default only the constraints in the jakarta.validation.groups.Default group run; a ?group=SomeGroup query parameter switches which validation group is checked, which lets a class carry both an always-on default set of constraints and optional stricter groups checked only in specific routes.

Because Bean Validator checks an already-deserialized POJO, it composes naturally after Chapter 10's unmarshal step — it is the complement to schema validation (validator: / json-validator:), which checks the raw wire bytes before or during unmarshalling, not after. The two catch different classes of problem: schema validation rejects a message that isn't shaped right at all; bean validation rejects one that parsed fine but violates a business constraint the schema itself doesn't express.

A Canonical Data Model (Hohpe & Woolf) is one integration-owned message format that every connected system's data is translated to and from. It trades a small, fixed per-system translation cost for eliminating direct format coupling between systems — turning what would be up to N(N-1) pairwise translators, if every system spoke every other system's format directly, into N translators, one per system, all aimed at the same shared shape.

Designing a canonical model is a modeling decision, not a technology choice: it means picking one shared representation for a business concept (an Order, a Customer) — field names, types, required-vs-optional, units — independent of any single source or downstream system's native format, then writing Message Translators (Chapter 09's setBody/bean/Processor, Chapter 10's marshal/unmarshal) at the edges to convert each system's format into and out of it.

Validation and the canonical model are complementary concerns, not the same one: validation decides whether an incoming message is well-formed and admissible at all (right shape, required fields present, values in range); the canonical model decides what shape a message gets translated into once it has been judged admissible. The common route shape is validate the raw incoming format at the edge, translate it to the canonical model, then let every downstream step trust that canonical shape without re-checking it.

The Validate EIP's failures and the schema-validator components' failures are distinct exception types — a failed validate() predicate throws PredicateValidationException, while the Validator and JSON Schema Validator components throw their own validation exception on a schema mismatch — so a route that uses more than one kind of check generally needs an onException clause for each, routing a rejected message to a dead-letter destination rather than letting the exception propagate and stop the route. Chapter 23 covers this onException/dead-letter machinery in full; this chapter only previews the shape.

snippets.note: validate() throws PredicateValidationException the instant a predicate fails. Unlike filter(), it never silently drops the message — the route stops with an exception unless something downstream catches it.
The raw XML string is checked against order.xsd before it is ever turned into an Order object — a separate step doing the same job JaxbDataFormat's own schema option offers inline.
json-validator is producer-only — always a .to() step in the middle of a route, never a route's from(...).
Bean Validator checks annotations on the already-deserialized POJO — the complement to schema validation, which runs against the raw wire bytes before or during unmarshal.
Catching the Validate EIP's specific exception type by name — the same onException shape Chapter 23 generalizes to every kind of route failure.

pitfalls: Reaching for validate() when the real need is schema validation — a predicate can check that a field exists or is positive, but it can't verify an entire message's structure against a contract the way an XSD or JSON Schema can; validate() is for a handful of business-rule checks, not a replacement for schema validation at the edge.

Validating a body with the wrong component for its format — validator: expects XML and a JAXP/XSD schema; json-validator: expects JSON and a JSON Schema document. Pointing either at the other format's body fails to validate anything meaningful, not because the data is invalid but because the wrong tool was asked to read it.

Unmarshalling first and validating second when the goal was to reject malformed input before it becomes a Java object — Chapter 09–10's type converters and data formats are often forgiving, and unmarshal(...) can salvage a partial or wrong-shaped object from malformed input rather than failing; schema validation meant to be a gate needs to run against the raw wire body, before or during unmarshal, not after.

Skipping bean validation because 'the JSON already matched the schema' — a JSON Schema and a set of Jakarta Bean Validation annotations often check different things (a schema checks the wire shape; @NotNull/@Size/custom constraints can encode business rules a schema doesn't express, like a total that must be positive), so the two are complementary checks at different points in the pipeline, not redundant ones.

Treating 'canonical model' as just 'the model already lying around' — a canonical model is deliberately independent of any one system's native format; modeling it directly off whichever system happened to be integrated first quietly turns it back into that system's format with extra steps, and the next new system to integrate pays the same combinatorial coupling cost the canonical model was supposed to eliminate.

claims.text: Choice (choice()/when()/otherwise()) is Camel's implementation of the Content-Based Router EIP: it reads one message and, without modifying it, decides which of several output channels it goes to — the same Message Router root pattern Chapter 03 introduced, specialized to route on content.

choice()/when()/otherwise() reads like a Java if/else-if/else ladder: each when(predicate) is tested in the order it's written, top to bottom, and the first one whose predicate evaluates true wins — its branch runs and no later when() or otherwise() is evaluated at all. There is no 'evaluate every branch and pick the best match'; it is a short-circuiting, order-sensitive chain, so branch order changes behavior whenever more than one predicate could match the same message.

when() accepts any Predicate or Expression, and like filter()/validate() before it, a bare string is parsed as a Simple expression by default — the same predicate machinery this book has used since Chapter 03, so header("x").isEqualTo(...) fluent builders and simple("${header.x} == 'y'") strings are interchangeable inside a when().

otherwise() is optional. If every when() predicate evaluates false and there is no otherwise() branch, the choice block simply does nothing — no branch executes, no exception is thrown — and the exchange falls through to whatever comes after the choice's .end() call. This is a common source of silently 'lost' messages: unlike Chapter 11's validate(), an unmatched choice is not an error by default, so an integration that expects every message to hit some branch needs an explicit otherwise() to catch the rest.

A choice() block is closed with .end() in the Java DSL, the same terminator used to close any nested block (splitter, multicast, etc.). Because Java's DSL is method-chained rather than naturally stack-based (unlike the YAML/XML DSLs), Camel cannot always infer which enclosing block a bare .end() should close; when another EIP that itself needs closing (e.g. loadBalance()) is nested directly inside a when()/otherwise(), Camel provides .endChoice() specifically to say 'return to the Choice's own scope' rather than closing the inner EIP a second time. This is a real, documented Java-DSL wrinkle — the YAML and XML DSLs don't need it, because their nesting is structural (indentation/elements), not chained method calls.

Filter (filter(predicate)) takes exactly one predicate and behaves like a plain Java if-block with nothing after it: a message whose predicate is true continues down the route past the filter; a message whose predicate is false is dropped where it stands — there is no 'else' destination, and dropping is silent, not an error. This is the opposite failure behavior from Chapter 11's validate(predicate), which throws PredicateValidationException on a false result — filter() says 'skip this one, no big deal', validate() says 'this one is wrong, and something needs to know.'

Filter implements the Message Filter EIP, which Hohpe & Woolf describe as a specialization of the Message Router that discards messages not meeting a criterion rather than routing them elsewhere — the same predicate machinery as choice()'s when(), just with an implicit 'drop' instead of an explicit second branch. A single-branch choice().when(pred).to(dest).otherwise().stop().end() is behaviorally close to a filter, but filter() is the idiomatic, more compact way to write 'continue only if' with no need for an explicit otherwise.

toD(expression) (Dynamic To) sends to an endpoint URI computed per exchange rather than fixed at route-build time — the expression (Simple by default) is evaluated against the current exchange and the result is used as the destination URI, e.g. toD("jms:queue:orders.${header.region}") resolves to a different concrete queue per message. This is a different kind of routing decision from choice(): choice()/when() picks among a small, fixed set of branches known when the route is written; toD() computes the destination itself, useful when the set of possible destinations isn't small or enumerable in the route's source (per-tenant queues, per-region endpoints).

toD() caches the resolved Endpoint/Producer per distinct URI it computes (via the producer cache) so that a repeated destination doesn't pay endpoint-resolution cost every message; the cacheSize option bounds how many distinct resolved endpoints/producers stay cached (0 = the default cache size, a negative value disables caching entirely). A highly dynamic URI (a queue name keyed by, say, per-order tenant ID with unbounded cardinality) can grow this cache without bound if left at defaults, which is the operational reason cacheSize exists.

The YAML DSL expresses the same choice/when/otherwise structure structurally rather than as chained method calls: a choice step holds a when list (each with its own predicate expression and its own steps) and an optional otherwise block with its own steps — there's no .end()/.endChoice() distinction in YAML because indentation, not method chaining, marks where a block ends.

snippets.note: the canonical choice()/when()/otherwise() shape; branches tested top to bottom, first match wins
filter() drops silently — contrast with validate() (Chapter 11), which throws
destination URI computed per exchange from a header; cacheSize bounds how many resolved endpoints/producers stay cached

- from:
    uri: direct:orders
    steps:
      - choice:
          when:
            - simple: "${header.OrderType} == 'DOMESTIC'"
              steps:
                - to: direct:domesticOrders
            - simple: "${header.OrderType} == 'INTERNATIONAL'"
              steps:
                - to: direct:internationalOrders
          otherwise:
            steps:
              - to: direct:unroutedOrders
snippets.note: same choice/when/otherwise structure in the YAML DSL — structural nesting, no .end()/.endChoice()

pitfalls: Forgetting otherwise() and assuming an unmatched message is an error — by default it silently falls through the choice block with no branch run and no exception.
Ordering when() branches so a broader/earlier predicate shadows a later, more specific one — evaluation is top-to-bottom, first-match-wins, so the more specific check must come first.

Nesting an EIP that needs its own .end() (e.g. loadBalance()) directly inside a when()/otherwise() and closing it with a plain .end() instead of .endChoice() — this closes the wrong scope and the next when()/otherwise() call won't compile against the Choice.
Confusing filter()'s silent drop with validate()'s (Chapter 11) thrown exception — swapping one for the other changes whether a rejected message disappears quietly or triggers exception-handling.
Leaving toD() at its default cache size against a destination URI with effectively unbounded cardinality (e.g. keyed by customer ID), letting the endpoint/producer cache grow without bound.

claims.text: The Splitter EIP (split()) breaks one incoming Exchange into many sub-Exchanges. Each sub-exchange is a copy of the original exchange with the body replaced by one part of the split result, so headers and properties set before the split are visible to every part.

split() accepts any Expression to decide how to cut the body up: tokenize(...) for delimited text (e.g. one line per message), xpath(...) for an XML node-set, jsonpath(...) for a JSON array, or simply body() when the body is already a java.util.Collection/array/Iterable/Iterator, which Camel splits element by element automatically with no extra expression needed.

By default split() runs non-streaming: it first materializes the full list of parts (so the total count is known up front), then processes each part in turn, holding all parts in memory. streaming() switches to on-demand splitting that produces and processes one part at a time without materializing the whole list first, trading lower memory use for not knowing the total part count in advance.

If split() is given no explicit AggregationStrategy, Camel defaults to UseLatestAggregationStrategy: the last sub-exchange processed simply becomes the outgoing exchange after the split() block, and every earlier sub-exchange's result is discarded. Without an explicit strategy, split() is a fan-out that throws away everything except whatever the final part produced.

Supplying a custom AggregationStrategy to split() lets each processed sub-exchange fold into a running result exchange inline, before the split() block completes. This inline recombination is a different mechanism from the standalone Aggregator EIP (aggregate()): it only ever combines the parts of the one exchange that was just split, in the same block, on the same thread of control (or a bounded set of parallel threads) as the split itself.

parallelProcessing() on split() processes sub-exchanges concurrently, but the calling thread still blocks at the split() block until every sub-exchange has finished before the route continues past it — parallelProcessing changes how the parts are processed, not whether the caller waits. When combined with a custom AggregationStrategy, that strategy's aggregate() method may then be invoked concurrently from multiple threads and must be implemented thread-safe; Camel synchronizes calls to aggregate() by default so it is safe (if serialized) even without that guarantee.

The Aggregator EIP (aggregate()) solves a different problem from split()'s inline recombination: it correlates and combines separate incoming Exchanges — which can arrive from many different route invocations over time, not necessarily from one split() call — into a single completed Exchange, grouped by a correlation Expression evaluated per exchange.

aggregate()'s AggregationStrategy has the same aggregate(Exchange oldExchange, Exchange newExchange) shape used by split(): oldExchange is null on the first exchange seen for a given correlation key (the strategy typically just returns newExchange to start the group), and on every later exchange for that same key, oldExchange holds the running aggregate built so far.

A correlation group completes — releasing its aggregated exchange downstream — under whichever configured completion condition fires first: completionSize(n) after n exchanges have joined that key; completionTimeout(ms), an inactivity timeout that resets every time a new exchange arrives for that key; completionInterval(ms), a fixed periodic sweep that completes whatever has accumulated regardless of per-key activity; or completionPredicate(...), evaluated against the aggregated exchange after each new arrival. completionTimeout and completionInterval cannot both be configured at the same time, but either can be combined with completionSize — whichever condition trips first wins for that key.

Aggregated state lives in a pluggable AggregationRepository. Camel's default is an in-memory repository, which loses every in-flight (not-yet-completed) group if the process restarts. A production aggregator that must survive a restart plugs in a persistent AggregationRepository implementation instead — Camel ships JDBC-, Infinispan-, and similar-backed options.

forceCompletionOnStop tells the aggregator to complete and release every in-flight group when the CamelContext stops, instead of leaving partially-aggregated groups stranded in the repository with no consumer left to complete them.

snippets.note: tokenize() splits a newline-delimited body into one sub-exchange per line; verified against the Splitter EIP reference (Camel 4.18.x).
split()'s own AggregationStrategy recombines the parts of one split message inline, in the same block — distinct from the standalone aggregate() EIP.
aggregate() correlates separately-arriving exchanges by header("orderId"); completionSize and completionTimeout are combined so whichever fires first releases the group.

pitfalls: split() without an explicit AggregationStrategy defaults to UseLatestAggregationStrategy, which silently keeps only the last sub-exchange's result and discards every earlier one — easy to miss because the route compiles and runs without error, it just quietly loses data.

Conflating split()'s inline AggregationStrategy with the standalone Aggregator EIP: the former only recombines the pieces of the one message just split, in one block; the latter correlates separate exchanges arriving over time by a correlation key. Reaching for aggregate() when split()'s own strategy would do (or vice versa) solves the wrong problem.

completionTimeout and completionInterval cannot both be set on the same aggregate() — they are two different notions of "done" (per-key inactivity vs. fixed periodic sweep) and picking the wrong one changes when a group actually completes.

Shipping the default in-memory AggregationRepository to production: any in-flight (not yet completed) correlation group is lost if the process restarts, silently dropping partially-aggregated data with no error at the time of loss.
